title: Types of diseases (communicable and non-communicable)
definition:
Disease is a condition that disturbs the normal functioning of the body. In Class 6 you learn that diseases can be grouped into two broad classes: those that spread from one person to another, and those that do not. The first kind is called a communicable disease, also known as an infectious disease. It is caused by tiny living organisms called pathogens that enter the body and produce an infection. These pathogens may travel through air, water, food, direct contact, or through carriers such as mosquitoes and flies. The second kind is called a non-communicable disease. It is not caused by a pathogen and it does not spread from person to person. It usually develops slowly and stays with the person who has it.

Communicable diseases are further classified by the type of pathogen that causes them. Bacterial diseases are caused by bacteria, which are very small single-celled organisms. Typhoid, which produces high fever and abdominal pain, and tuberculosis, which usually affects the lungs, are important bacterial diseases. Viral diseases are caused by viruses, which are even smaller and can only multiply inside a living cell. The common cold, measles and chickenpox are familiar viral diseases. Protozoal diseases are caused by protozoa, which are one-celled animals. The best known example in India is malaria, caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and spread by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. Diseases caused by worms, such as tapeworm infection and elephantiasis, are also communicable because the worms enter the body and can spread from one host to another.

Non-communicable diseases, on the other hand, are not caused by living organisms. Diabetes, in which the body cannot control the level of sugar in the blood, asthma, which makes breathing difficult, and heart disease, which affects the working of the heart, are common examples. These diseases may be influenced by genetic factors, poor diet, lack of exercise, or harmful habits, but they cannot be passed from person to person like a cold.

The two types can be distinguished by a few clear features. Communicable diseases are infectious, they are caused by pathogens, they spread from an infected person to a healthy person, and they can often be prevented by clean water, clean air, personal hygiene and vaccination. Non-communicable diseases are non-infectious, they are not caused by pathogens, they do not spread, and they are usually managed by lifestyle changes and long-term treatment. The key rule to remember is: if a pathogen can travel to a new person, the disease is communicable; if it cannot, it is non-communicable.
textWalkthrough:
Think back to what you studied in the previous class, in node c5_bio_008. You learned about deficiency diseases such as night-blindness, scurvy and rickets. Those diseases happen because the body lacks something -- a particular vitamin or mineral. The cause is inside the body, not a living organism. You also revised the idea that clean surroundings and public health protect people from illness. Now you are ready for the next step: some diseases are not caused by what you lack, but by tiny organisms that spread to you from another person, from water, food, air or insects. This is the world of communicable diseases.

Let us begin with the simplest question: how do you know a disease is communicable? Imagine two children sitting next to each other in class. If one has a cold and sneezes, tiny droplets carrying the cold virus may enter the other child's nose. A few days later, the second child also has a runny nose and sneezing. That is a communicable disease. It is contagious, because it passes from person to person. A non-communicable disease is different. If one child has diabetes, no amount of sitting together, sharing lunch or playing will make the other child diabetic. The disease stays with the person who has it, just like a broken pencil stays with its owner. This is the most important difference you must keep in mind for the board exam: spread versus no spread.

Now, how do we sort communicable diseases? We sort them by the kind of pathogen. First come bacterial diseases. Bacteria are single-celled living things, much smaller than the cells of your body. They can cause typhoid, which gives fever, headache and sometimes a rash, and tuberculosis, which mainly attacks the lungs. A strong answer in the exam would name the disease and its cause: "Typhoid is caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi." A weak answer just says "Typhoid is caused by germs," because "germs" is too vague and may not earn the mark. Next are viral diseases. Viruses are tinier than bacteria and cannot live or multiply on their own; they need to enter your cells. The common cold, measles and chickenpox are viral. A good answer is "The common cold is caused by a virus such as the rhinovirus." A poor answer is "The common cold is caused by bacteria," which many students write and is wrong. Then we have protozoal diseases. The name sounds difficult, but you already know the most important one: malaria. In India, malaria is a serious problem in many rural and forested areas, especially in states with heavy monsoon rain and stagnant water. The protozoan Plasmodium enters the human blood when a female Anopheles mosquito bites. Finally, diseases caused by worms, such as tapeworm infection and elephantiasis, belong to the communicable group because the worms travel from one host to another.

Let us look at non-communicable diseases more closely. Diabetes is common in India and is linked to diet and family history. Asthma is a breathing problem that may run in families or be triggered by dust and pollen. Heart disease may develop because of high blood pressure, smoking or lack of exercise. A good answer describes one of these and adds that it does not spread. A bad answer says "Asthma spreads when a person coughs near you," which is a common confusion. It does not.

To do well in the ICSE/ISC board exam, examiners expect you to present the classification clearly, often in a table with columns for "Disease" and "Causative organism." They also expect the exact name of the pathogen where the syllabus requires it. Make sure you do not mix up bacterial and viral diseases, and remember that antibiotics work against bacteria, not against viruses. Keep your examples Indian and real, and you will score well.
eli5: Some sicknesses are like shared snacks: they move from one person to another, so we call them communicable. Tiny germs called bacteria, viruses or protozoa cause them. Other sicknesses are like a sore knee: they stay with one person and do not move, so we call them non-communicable. Eating well, staying clean and using safe water help stop the first kind, while good habits help manage the second kind.
misconceptionText:
Mistake 1 -- Using the wrong name or category for the disease. board examiners have observed that candidates often mention disease names that do not match the question, such as writing dengue or chikungunya when the answer should be a specific disease, or confusing the symptoms of one disease with another. At Class 6, this appears when students say "malaria is a bacterial disease" or "typhoid is caused by a virus." The correction is to keep a ready table: typhoid and tuberculosis are bacterial; common cold, measles and chickenpox are viral; malaria is protozoal; tapeworm and elephantiasis are worm diseases. Check the cause before you write the answer.

Mistake 2 -- Mixing up medicine and treatment. Examiners noted that students often confuse "antibody" with "antibiotic" and write names such as penicillin where they should not. In the same way, Class 6 students may think antibiotics cure a cold or malaria. The correction is to remember that antibiotics work against bacteria, not against viruses or protozoa. The common cold and measles are viral, so antibiotics do not help; typhoid is bacterial, so a doctor may prescribe antibiotics.

Mistake 3 -- Confusing tests and modes of spread. Examiners saw candidates writing "Widal test" for diseases it does not diagnose, or giving vague answers like "a blood test" for every disease. At this level, the correction is to link the test to the cause: the Widal test is used for typhoid, a bacterial disease; malaria is detected by looking for the Plasmodium parasite in blood; and a disease that spreads through mosquito bites must be prevented by stopping mosquitoes, not by medicines alone.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Classify the following diseases as communicable or non-communicable and give the correct causative organism or factor for each: typhoid, common cold, malaria, diabetes, tapeworm infection. Write your answer in two clear columns.
Answer: Typhoid is a communicable disease caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi; it spreads through contaminated food and water. The common cold is communicable and is caused by a virus such as the rhinovirus; it spreads through tiny droplets released when an infected person sneezes or coughs. Malaria is communicable, caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, and is spread by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito, which is common in parts of India with stagnant water. Tapeworm infection is also communicable, caused by the tapeworm, and spreads when a person eats undercooked meat or food contaminated with the worm's eggs. Diabetes is non-communicable; it is not caused by a pathogen and does not spread from one person to another. It occurs when the body cannot control blood sugar, often because of diet, lifestyle or family history. This shows how the same list of illnesses can be sorted first by whether they spread, and then by what causes them.

Q2 (reasoning): Rohan had a high fever and his doctor said it was typhoid. His sister had a runny nose and the doctor said it was a common cold. Both had infections, so why did the doctor prescribe antibiotics for Rohan but not for his sister?
Answer: The doctor made different choices because the two illnesses are caused by different kinds of pathogens. Typhoid is a bacterial disease, and antibiotics are medicines that can kill bacteria or stop them from growing. Therefore, antibiotics can help fight the Salmonella typhi bacteria that cause typhoid. The common cold, on the other hand, is a viral disease. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses because viruses are not living cells in the same way as bacteria; they multiply inside human cells, and antibiotics cannot reach them. Giving antibiotics for a cold would not cure it and could even be harmful by encouraging the bacteria in the body to become resistant to the medicine. This is why the doctor did not prescribe antibiotics for the cold, but did prescribe them for typhoid. It is a good example of how understanding the cause of a disease helps us choose the right treatment.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says: "All communicable diseases can be stopped if we keep our surroundings clean, but non-communicable diseases cannot be prevented at all." Is this statement correct? Give a balanced argument.
Answer: The statement is only partly true and is wrong in both parts if taken absolutely. It is true that keeping surroundings clean can prevent many communicable diseases. Clean water, safe food, good sewage disposal and hygienic habits stop diseases such as typhoid, cholera and many worm infections. Controlling mosquitoes by removing stagnant water can also reduce malaria. However, not all communicable diseases can be stopped by cleanliness alone. Some, like the common cold and measles, spread through droplets in the air and through direct contact, so even clean surroundings may not fully stop them. Vaccination and avoiding close contact are also needed. On the other hand, the claim that non-communicable diseases cannot be prevented at all is also wrong. Diabetes, heart disease and asthma may not spread from person to person, but they can often be prevented or delayed by a healthy diet, regular exercise, avoiding tobacco and alcohol, and controlling stress. For example, eating less sugar and staying active can lower the risk of diabetes. Therefore, both kinds of disease can be reduced, but the methods are different: communicable diseases are prevented mainly by hygiene, vaccination and controlling vectors, while non-communicable diseases are prevented mainly by healthy lifestyle choices. The statement ignores these important facts.

Q4 (apply): In a village in Odisha, several children develop fever with chills every alternate day during the rainy season. A large puddle has formed near the school. Identify the likely disease, its causative organism, how it spreads, and suggest two practical prevention steps for the village.
Answer: The likely disease is malaria. Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and is spread from person to person through the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. These mosquitoes breed in stagnant water, so the large puddle near the school is the perfect breeding place. During the rainy season, puddles and ponds collect water, and the number of mosquitoes increases. The children are probably being bitten at night or in the early evening. Two practical steps the village can take are: first, drain the puddle or fill it with soil so that mosquitoes cannot lay eggs in the water; second, encourage the children to sleep under mosquito nets and wear long-sleeved clothes in the evening. These steps reduce the breeding of mosquitoes and protect the children from bites, which are the main mode of spread for malaria in such an area.

Q5 (create): Design a poster titled "Stop the Spread!" for your school noticeboard. It should have two columns: one showing habits that prevent communicable diseases, and another showing habits that increase the risk. Explain what you would draw and write in each column, and which one disease from this node you would highlight.
Answer: In the left column, I would draw bright pictures of healthy habits that prevent communicable diseases: a child washing hands with soap, a family drinking boiled water, a person covering the mouth and nose while sneezing, a child sleeping under a mosquito net, and a student eating freshly cooked food from a clean tiffin. Below each picture I would write short captions such as "Wash hands before eating," "Drink safe water," "Cover your cough," "Use a mosquito net" and "Eat clean, cooked food." In the right column I would draw the opposite habits in duller colours: a child drinking water from a roadside tap, uncovered food left in the open, someone sneezing without covering the mouth, a child playing near a stagnant puddle, and a person sharing a handkerchief. The captions would read "Unsafe water," "Uncovered food," "Coughing openly," "Stagnant water breeds mosquitoes" and "Sharing personal items." I would highlight malaria at the bottom of the poster, because it is an important communicable disease in India and the Anopheles mosquito's link to stagnant water is easy to show. The poster would make students see that small daily choices decide whether disease spreads or stops.
masteryCriteria: Can define communicable (spread from person to person: flu, malaria) and non-communicable (do not spread: diabetes, heart disease) diseases with two examples each; can state one key difference between them.

title: Modes of disease transmission
definition: Disease transmission is the process by which an infectious agent, or pathogen, passes from an infected person or source to a healthy person and causes a new infection. The route through which the pathogen travels is called the mode of transmission, and for the diseases you study in Class 6 these routes are grouped into four main types: airborne, waterborne, foodborne, and vector-borne. Each route depends on where the germ lives, how it leaves the body of the infected person, and how it enters the body of a new host. Airborne transmission occurs when an infected person coughs or sneezes and produces tiny droplets that carry germs through the air; another person nearby may breathe in these droplets and become infected. Common cold and influenza are familiar examples of airborne diseases. Waterborne transmission occurs when disease-causing germs enter a source of drinking water, usually through contamination with human faeces or urine, and a person drinks this water without boiling or filtering it. Cholera and typhoid are classic waterborne diseases, especially during floods or where sewage mixes with wells. Foodborne transmission occurs when food is prepared or stored in unclean conditions, when it is handled by unwashed hands, or when it is spoiled and allowed to harbour multiplying germs; eating such food can lead to food poisoning or diarrhoea. Vector-borne transmission occurs when an insect, such as a mosquito, picks up the germ from an infected person or animal and injects it into another person while biting. Malaria, spread by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, and dengue, spread by the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito, are important vector-borne diseases in India. Understanding the mode of transmission is the first step toward prevention, because once you know how a germ travels you can block that pathway by covering your mouth while coughing or sneezing, drinking boiled or filtered water, eating clean and freshly prepared food, using mosquito nets and repellents, keeping personal hygiene, and avoiding close contact with people who are already infected.
textWalkthrough:
Before you begin, remember what you learned in the earlier node c5_bio_023, where you saw that unclean surroundings can cause disease: mosquitoes breeding in stagnant water can spread dengue and malaria, contaminated water can cause cholera, and dirty hands can cause diarrhoea. You already know that some diseases come from germs around us, but now, in this node, you are going to organise that knowledge into a proper system. You are moving from simply knowing that dirty water and mosquitoes can make you sick to understanding that diseases travel through four clear pathways: air, water, food, and insect vectors.

Let us begin with the direct prerequisite node c6_bio_020, where you met the three kinds of causative agents of communicable diseases: bacteria, viruses, and protozoa. Keep those names in mind, because different agents usually prefer different routes. A bacterium that causes cholera moves through water, a virus that causes influenza travels through air, and a protozoan that causes malaria needs a mosquito vector. So the type of germ gives you a strong hint about how it will spread.

Now picture a child with the common cold sitting in a classroom in a city like Kolkata or Chennai. When the child coughs or sneezes without covering the mouth, tiny droplets shoot out, carrying the cold virus into the air. A classmate nearby can breathe in those droplets and catch the cold. This is airborne transmission. A good way to answer a board question is to say that the common cold and influenza spread through tiny droplets released into the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. A weak answer would simply say that the disease is in the air all the time; that is not true, because the germs need a source, usually an infected person, and they travel only a short distance in droplets.

Next, think about a village in Bihar or Uttar Pradesh after the monsoon. If a well or a hand-pump is not protected, floodwater carrying sewage can seep into the drinking water. If someone drinks this water without boiling or filtering it, the cholera bacteria or typhoid germs enter the body and cause disease. This is waterborne transmission. A strong answer names the disease and the exact source: cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated drinking water. A weak answer just says dirty water causes disease, without naming the disease or explaining how the water became unsafe.

Foodborne transmission is similar but different. Imagine a plate of chaat or cut fruit sold on a roadside in Delhi or Mumbai. If the seller used unwashed hands, left the food uncovered, or used spoiled ingredients, germs can multiply in the food. When someone eats it, the germs cause food poisoning or diarrhoea. A good answer explains that food poisoning and diarrhoea are spread by eating contaminated or spoiled food. A weak answer only says that bad food makes you sick.

Finally, think of the hot and rainy season in a village in Kerala or Assam. Puddles of stagnant water become breeding places for mosquitoes. When a female Anopheles mosquito bites a person with malaria, it carries the Plasmodium protozoan and injects it into the next person it bites. Dengue is spread similarly, but by a different mosquito, Aedes aegypti, which bites during the daytime and breeds in clean stagnant water. This is vector-borne transmission. A strong answer names the exact vector, such as the female Anopheles mosquito for malaria; a weak answer just writes mosquito, which does not show that you understand the difference between the insects.

For the ICSE/ISC board exam, examiners expect you to match the disease with its mode of transmission accurately and to use the correct scientific terms. They notice when students use vague words like bacteria or virus without giving the specific transmission route, or when they confuse one mosquito with another. So always name the route, the example, and, for vector-borne diseases, the correct insect. When you are asked about prevention, do not just list good habits; connect each habit to a mode of transmission, showing that you understand why it works.
eli5: Germs are tiny living things that can make us sick. Sometimes they travel through the air when someone coughs, through water when it is dirty, through food when it is spoiled, or through a mosquito bite. To stop them, cover your cough, drink clean water, eat fresh food, sleep under a net, and wash your hands.
misconceptionText:
One common mistake is to use the general words bacteria or virus without explaining the actual mode of transmission. board examiners have observed that many candidates write general terms like bacteria and virus instead of giving the precise route, such as through air, through water, through food, or through an insect vector. Remember that the question usually wants the pathway, not only the kind of germ.

Another frequent error is to call every mosquito the carrier of every mosquito-borne disease. Examiners note that candidates often write Anopheles or Aedes mosquito, or simply mosquito, without being specific. Malaria is carried by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, while dengue is carried by the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. Writing only mosquito shows that you do not know the difference and may lose marks.

A third misunderstanding is to think that food and water always cause the same diseases in the same way. Some students say that cholera is caused by eating contaminated food and typhoid by drinking contaminated water, or mix the two. In reality, cholera and typhoid are mainly waterborne, although they can sometimes be foodborne if food is washed with contaminated water, while food poisoning and diarrhoea are mainly linked to contaminated or spoiled food. Always name the correct mode and the correct example together.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): List the four main modes of disease transmission and give one example of a disease for each mode.
Answer: The four main modes of disease transmission are transmission through air, through water, through food, and through insects or vectors. Transmission through air takes place when an infected person coughs or sneezes and releases tiny droplets carrying germs into the air; examples include the common cold and influenza. Transmission through water occurs when a person drinks water that has been contaminated by germs from the faeces or urine of an infected person; cholera and typhoid are common waterborne diseases. Transmission through food occurs when a person eats food that has been handled with dirty hands, stored in unhygienic conditions, or allowed to spoil; food poisoning and diarrhoea are typical examples. Transmission through insects or vectors occurs when an insect, usually a mosquito, carries germs from one person to another through its bite; malaria, spread by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, and dengue, spread by the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito, are important examples. Naming all four modes and one disease for each shows that you understand the system.

Q2 (reasoning): Explain why cholera and typhoid are more common in villages and cities that do not have safe drinking water and proper sewage disposal.
Answer: Cholera and typhoid are both waterborne diseases, which means they are mainly transmitted when a person drinks water that has been contaminated with germs from the faeces or urine of an infected person. In villages and cities that do not have safe drinking water and proper sewage disposal, human waste can easily mix with the sources of drinking water. For example, if a latrine is too close to a well, or if sewage drains into a river from which people draw water, the germs enter the water supply. During the monsoon, floodwater can carry sewage into open wells and ponds, making the problem worse. If people drink this water without boiling or filtering it, the germs reach their intestines and cause infection. The reason these diseases become more common is that the contaminated water provides a fast and continuous pathway for the germs to travel from one infected person to many healthy people. Preventing the disease therefore depends on protecting the water source, treating the water by boiling or filtering, and disposing of sewage safely so that it cannot mix with drinking water.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "If we always keep our windows open, no airborne disease can ever enter our room." Evaluate this statement and explain whether you agree or it is only partly true.
Answer: This statement is only partly true and can be misleading if it is taken too far. It is true that fresh air and good ventilation can reduce the concentration of germs in the air, because moving air disperses the tiny droplets released by coughing and sneezing and carries some of them away. In a well-ventilated room, an airborne disease like the common cold or influenza is less likely to spread than in a closed, crowded room where the same air is breathed again and again. However, keeping windows open does not block airborne diseases completely. If an infected person is sitting close to the window, the droplets from a cough or sneeze can still travel directly to another person nearby before the wind can carry them away. Also, the effect of open windows depends on the direction of the wind, the size of the room, the number of people, and the weather; in very cold or rainy conditions, people cannot keep windows open all the time. Moreover, many airborne diseases can also spread through close contact or by touching surfaces that have droplets on them, so ventilation alone is not enough. The best protection is to combine good ventilation with covering the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing, avoiding close contact with infected persons, and maintaining personal hygiene. Therefore, open windows help, but they are not a complete guarantee against airborne infection.

Q4 (apply): You live in a village in West Bengal where water collects in paddy fields and small ponds during the monsoon. Suggest three practical measures to reduce the spread of malaria in your village during this season.
Answer: Malaria is a vector-borne disease that is transmitted through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, and these mosquitoes often breed in stagnant water. In a West Bengal village with paddy fields and ponds, the first practical measure would be to prevent water from stagnating, or at least to manage it, by filling potholes, draining ditches, and introducing fish such as guppy that eat mosquito larvae. The second measure would be to protect people from mosquito bites by sleeping under insecticide-treated mosquito nets, using mosquito repellents in the evening, and wearing clothes that cover the arms and legs. The third measure would be to keep the area around homes clean and free of old tyres, broken pots, and other containers that can hold rainwater, because even small collections of clean stagnant water are enough for Anopheles mosquitoes to breed. These three measures together attack the problem at both ends: they reduce the number of mosquitoes and they protect people from being bitten.

Q5 (create): Design a one-day school programme to teach younger students how to prevent communicable diseases at home and in school.
Answer: The programme could be called Healthy Habits Day and would be run by Class 6 students for younger children. The morning could begin with a short play in the assembly showing four scenes: a child who covers the mouth while coughing, a family drinking boiled and filtered water, a student eating clean and freshly packed food, and a child sleeping under a mosquito net. After the play, the school could be divided into four activity stations, one for each mode of transmission. At the air station, students would practise coughing into the elbow and learn why droplets spread germs. At the water station, they would see a simple filter and learn about boiling. At the food station, they would identify clean versus spoiled food from pictures and learn about washing hands before eating. At the vector station, they would see a model of a mosquito net and learn to empty stagnant water. In the afternoon, each child could make a small poster of one healthy habit to take home, and the day could close with a pledge: cover, clean, cook, filter, and net. This programme would make the prevention of communicable diseases easy to remember and would help students become health ambassadors in their own families.
masteryCriteria: Can name four modes of disease transmission (air: flu, water: cholera, contact: ringworm, vector: malaria); can state one way to prevent each mode (mask, clean water, hygiene, mosquito nets); can match a disease to its transmission mode.

title: Hygiene and sanitation
definition:
Hygiene and sanitation are two closely linked practices that protect people, homes and communities from infection and disease by removing the conditions in which germs thrive. Hygiene is the set of personal and domestic habits that keep the body and living space clean: washing hands before meals and after using the toilet, bathing regularly, trimming nails, wearing clean clothes, brushing teeth and storing food and water safely. Sanitation is the wider community-level system that keeps waste, sewage and garbage from contaminating the surroundings: providing covered dustbins, sweeping roads and courtyards, cleaning drains, building and maintaining toilets, treating drinking water, composting biodegradable waste and recycling materials such as paper, glass, metal and certain plastics. When hygiene and sanitation work together, they break the transmission routes of many diseases that move through air, water, food and insects.

Keeping surroundings clean begins with regular cleaning of rooms, kitchens, bathrooms, courtyards, streets and school compounds. It also means proper waste segregation, which is the practice of sorting garbage at the point where it is made into separate bins for biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste so that each type can be handled correctly. Drains must be kept clear because stagnant water and blocked drains become breeding places for mosquitoes and allow dirty water to spread contamination. Safe disposal of garbage requires the use of covered dustbins, composting of biodegradable waste such as vegetable peels, fruit scraps and garden leaves, recycling of dry waste and a firm decision to avoid littering in public places such as parks, bus stands and railway tracks.

Healthy hygiene practices are the everyday actions that stop germs from entering the body. Washing hands before eating and after visiting the toilet removes harmful microbes picked from surfaces, food waste and faeces. Bathing regularly washes away sweat, dirt and bacteria from the skin, while trimmed nails prevent germs from collecting under them. Wearing clean clothes and keeping footwear clean also reduce contact with dust and disease-causing particles. In Indian homes, many families still boil drinking water in the kitchen before storing it in clean pots, much like using a strainer to catch impurities, because heat kills the hidden germs that even clear-looking water may carry.

Non-communicable diseases are long-term conditions that are not passed from one person to another and include diabetes, hypertension and obesity. These diseases develop slowly because of unbalanced eating, lack of physical activity and unhealthy lifestyle choices. Prevention depends on a balanced diet that includes cereals, pulses, vegetables, fruit and milk, regular exercise such as walking, cycling or playing games and avoiding junk food, processed snacks and too much salt or sugar. The importance of sanitation for public health is clear from large Indian programmes: the Swachh Bharat Mission promoted toilet construction, Indore became one of India's cleanest cities through strict door-to-door waste segregation, Ambikapur in Chhattisgarh turned waste management into a women-led recycling enterprise and many schools and villages run compost pits that turn kitchen waste into manure. When an entire neighbourhood follows good hygiene and sanitation, the whole community becomes healthier.
textWalkthrough:
Imagine you are walking through the ideas you have already studied. In node c5_bio_023 you learned personal hygiene habits such as hand washing, bathing, wearing clean clothes and keeping nails trimmed, and you saw how dirty surroundings can lead to diseases such as dengue, malaria, cholera and skin infections. Then in c6_bio_021 you looked closely at how diseases actually spread from one person to another through air, water, food and insects. Now, in c6_bio_022, you are taking the next step: you are moving from "I keep myself clean so I do not catch a disease" to "We keep our surroundings clean so the whole neighbourhood stays healthy."

Let us begin with the idea of keeping surroundings clean. Think about your own home first. If you sweep the rooms, wipe kitchen counters and clean the bathroom every day, you remove dust, food scraps and germs before they can grow. But cleaning is not enough on its own. A good household also separates its waste. Kitchen waste such as vegetable peels, leftover rice and fruit skins are biodegradable; they can rot naturally and be turned into compost. Plastic wrappers, glass bottles, metal foil and old newspapers are non-biodegradable; they should be given to a recycler or placed in a dry-waste bin. If these two types of waste are mixed, the wet waste makes the dry waste dirty, the whole bin starts smelling and neither can be used again. Keeping drains clean is just as important, especially during the monsoon in places like Mumbai and Kolkata, where blocked drains can hold dirty water and allow mosquitoes to breed.

Now think about safe garbage disposal. A weak answer might simply say, "Put garbage in a dustbin," but a strong answer explains the whole chain: use a covered dustbin so that flies cannot reach rotting waste; carry the waste to the municipal collection point at the right time; let biodegradable waste become compost in a pit or a home composter; send paper, glass, plastic and metal for recycling; and put only what cannot be reused into a properly managed landfill or incinerator. A weak answer may also say, "Throw it anywhere because the sweeper will pick it up," but a strong answer knows that littering spreads germs, spoils the look of public spaces and harms animals. In cities such as Indore, the success of cleanliness drives comes from citizens putting waste into the right coloured bins at the right time.

Healthy hygiene practices are the personal part of the story. They are not new to you, but this year you are asked to connect them to disease prevention more clearly. Washing hands before meals removes germs that come from door handles, books, coins and soil. Washing hands after the toilet is even more important because human waste can carry germs that cause diarrhoea and typhoid. Bathing daily removes sweat and bacteria from the skin, and keeping nails short stops germs from hiding underneath them. Wearing clean clothes means the fabric does not carry dust and stale sweat back to the body. These habits become powerful when everyone around you also follows them, because one careless person can pass germs to many others.

Next comes a topic that is different in nature: non-communicable diseases. In c6_bio_021 you learned about diseases that spread from person to person, but diabetes, hypertension and obesity do not spread through touch, air or water. They develop inside the body over months and years because of too much junk food, too little exercise, too much stress and an unbalanced diet. A weak answer might say, "These diseases happen because of germs," but a strong answer says, "They can be prevented by a balanced diet, regular physical activity and avoiding processed and fried food." A plate that has rice or chapati, a dal or egg, vegetables, a little curd and a fruit is far better for long-term health than a packet of chips, a fizzy drink and a burger.

Finally, why does all this matter for public health? When a whole town practises good sanitation, the water in its rivers and wells stays cleaner, mosquitoes find fewer breeding sites and hospitals see fewer cases of preventable disease. The board examiners often notice that students write vague answers such as "keep surroundings clean" without giving the specific measures. To earn marks, you must name those measures: regular sweeping, covered dustbins, waste segregation, composting, recycling, drain cleaning and toilet use. The board expects you to show that you can list the practices and explain how they stop disease from spreading.
eli5: Hygiene and sanitation mean keeping your body, home and neighbourhood clean so germs cannot make you sick. You wash your hands, have a bath, wear clean clothes and put rubbish in the right bin. The community keeps drains and streets clean, turns food waste into compost and recycles useful things. When everyone does this, fewer people fall ill and everyone stays healthier.
misconceptionText:
One common mistake is to give vague, one-line answers such as "keep clean" without naming the specific hygiene or sanitation measures that the examiner wants. board examiners noticed this pattern clearly: in the board exam analysis, candidates wrote "keeping surrounding clean" but omitted solid and liquid waste management and the construction of toilets, so the remedy was to review the topic fundamentals. The correction is to write a precise list that includes daily sweeping, covered dustbins, waste segregation into biodegradable and non-biodegradable, composting, drain cleaning and safe water practices, and to explain how each one stops contamination.

A second error is to treat hygiene as a purely personal issue and forget community sanitation. Some students list hand washing and bathing but leave out drain cleaning, garbage disposal and recycling. This matches the examiner concern seen in related answers where candidates were expected to give specific measures such as feed, protection, disease, doctor, cleanliness and care, but produced only partial responses. The correction is to include both personal habits and community systems, because infection can enter the body through the air, water, food and insects that surround us.

A third error is to confuse non-communicable diseases with communicable infections. Because students have just studied how germs pass from person to person, they sometimes think that diabetes, hypertension and obesity also spread by contact. The correction is to remember that non-communicable diseases are not caused by germs; they develop slowly because of diet, exercise and lifestyle, so preventing them means eating a balanced diet, taking regular physical activity and avoiding junk food rather than using hand washing or medicines alone.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): List four ways to keep your surroundings clean and explain briefly why each one is useful.
Answer: The first way is regular sweeping and washing of floors, courtyards and bathrooms, because removing dust, food scraps and spilt liquids takes away the places where germs breed and insects feed. The second way is proper waste segregation, which means putting biodegradable kitchen waste in a green bin and non-biodegradable dry waste such as plastic, paper and glass in a separate bin, so that each type can be handled properly without contaminating the other. The third way is keeping drains and gutters clear, because blocked drains hold dirty water that becomes a breeding ground for mosquitoes and can spread contamination onto streets and into homes. The fourth way is using covered dustbins in kitchens, classrooms and public places, because lids stop flies, cockroaches and stray animals from carrying germs from the garbage to food and people. Together these four actions reduce the chance of infection in the home and the neighbourhood.

Q2 (reasoning): Why must biodegradable and non-biodegradable wastes be thrown into different bins before they are collected?
Answer: Biodegradable waste such as vegetable peels, fruit skins, leftover food and garden leaves can be broken down naturally by bacteria and fungi, so it is best turned into compost that enriches the soil. Non-biodegradable waste such as plastic wrappers, metal foil, glass bottles and old newspapers does not rot easily, but much of it can be cleaned, processed and used again through recycling. If these two kinds of waste are mixed, the wet biodegradable waste spoils the dry recyclable material, making it dirty and worthless; it also produces a bad smell and a liquid called leachate that can pollute soil and water. Separate bins also help municipal workers, kabadiwalas and composting plants do their work quickly and safely, so segregation is the first and most important step in safe garbage disposal.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "As long as I wash my hands, I do not need to bother about where the garbage goes." Evaluate this statement.
Answer: This statement is only partly correct and is mostly weak. Washing hands before meals and after using the toilet is one of the most important personal hygiene habits because it removes germs that can enter the body through food, drink or touch, and it certainly lowers the risk of stomach infections and respiratory illnesses. However, the student ignores the fact that disease can reach the body in many other ways even if one's own hands are clean. Uncovered dustbins attract flies, which can carry germs from garbage to uncovered food; blocked drains breed mosquitoes that spread dengue and malaria; contaminated water from poor sanitation causes cholera and typhoid; and rotting garbage on the street releases bacteria into the air. The person who throws waste into the right bin and keeps drains clean is helping to break the same disease routes that hand washing breaks at a personal level. Therefore, personal hand washing and community sanitation are both necessary, and neither can replace the other. A truly healthy neighbourhood needs both.

Q4 (apply): Your school wants to start a "Clean Campus" drive. Describe the practical steps you would take, including how you would handle solid waste and keep the drains safe.
Answer: The first step would be to place colour-coded dustbins across the campus: a green bin for biodegradable waste such as food scraps and fallen leaves, a blue bin for non-biodegradable dry waste such as paper, plastic and glass, and a red bin for hazardous waste such as used batteries or broken laboratory glass. Each bin should have a lid to keep away flies and animals. The second step would be to start a small compost pit or vermicompost unit in the school garden for the biodegradable waste, and to arrange for a local recycler to collect the dry waste every week. The third step would be to form student teams for daily sweeping, classroom cleaning and drain inspection, making sure that leaves, plastic bags and food wrappers do not block the water channels. The fourth step would be to put up posters and hold short assemblies that explain why hand washing, clean clothes and covered dustbins prevent disease. Finally, the school should keep a record of attendance, waterlogging, water storage and cleanliness so that the drive improves week by week.

Q5 (create): Design a poster and a three-point action plan for your neighbourhood to keep its local market clean during a festival.
Answer: The poster would show a picture of a busy market with a bright, smiling community on one side and piles of rotting garbage, flies and blocked drains on the other side, with a bold slogan such as "Clean Market, Healthy Celebrations." Under the slogan it would list three simple messages: throw waste only into covered dustbins, keep food stalls away from open drains, and wash hands before serving or eating food. The three-point action plan would begin with setting up enough covered dustbins at the entrance and exit of the market, and asking each stall owner to keep a small bin for dry and wet waste. The second point would be to hire a team to sweep the market twice a day and to clear any drain blockages immediately, especially after rain. The third point would be to arrange a composting corner for fruit and vegetable waste and to send paper, plastic and metal for recycling instead of dumping it by the roadside. With these steps, the festival can be enjoyed without creating a health hazard for shoppers, hawkers and nearby homes.
masteryCriteria: Can list five hygiene and sanitation practices (handwashing, safe water, toilet use, waste disposal, food hygiene); can state two diseases prevented by each practice (diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid); can explain why sanitation is important for public health.

title: Allergy concept and allergens
definition: An allergy is a condition in which the body's immune system overreacts to substances that are normally harmless to most people. In simple terms, the immune system, which is the body's defence army, treats an ordinary substance as if it were a dangerous enemy. This false alarm causes reactions such as sneezing, coughing, runny nose, watering eyes, skin rash, or itching. The substance that causes this reaction is called an allergen. Allergens are not germs, and they do not cause infections, but the body mistakenly identifies them as threats and releases chemicals like histamine, which produces the uncomfortable symptoms of an allergy. Common allergens in the environment around us include dust, tiny particles called pollen grains that come from flowers and grasses, dust mites, strong sunlight, and certain food items such as shellfish and nuts. Each allergen can enter the body through different routes. When a person eats something he or she is sensitive to, the allergen enters through the mouth. When dust or pollen floats in the air and is breathed in, it enters through the nose. When the skin touches something irritating, such as certain plants, fabrics, or chemicals, the allergen enters through the skin. It is important to understand the difference between an allergen and an allergy. The allergen is the trigger, the thing that starts the problem. The allergy is the body's response, the set of symptoms that appear after contact with the allergen. For example, dust is the allergen, but sneezing and a runny nose are the allergy. Pollen is the allergen, but watering eyes and sneezing are the allergy. Food such as shellfish is the allergen, but a rash or stomach discomfort is the allergy. In Indian contexts, children may come across dust from old books in school libraries, pollen from neem or parthenium plants in neighbourhoods, dust mites in bedding and carpets, and strong sunlight during outdoor activities in summer. Sensitivity to particular food items, such as peanuts, cashew nuts, or prawns, is also commonly observed. The concept of histamine helps explain why the symptoms appear: when the immune system detects an allergen, it releases histamine, which makes the blood vessels widen and causes swelling, itching, and other signs of an allergic reaction. Therefore, learning about allergy means understanding the role of the immune system, the examples of allergens, the entry routes through the nose, mouth, and skin, and the clear distinction between the trigger and the reaction.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin by remembering what you studied in Class 6 under the node c6_bio_020. You learned about communicable diseases, which are illnesses caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa. You understood that germs can spread from one person to another through air, water, food, or contact, and that the body's immune system fights these invaders to keep us healthy. That background is essential because now, in Class 7, we take the next step. We are going to learn that the immune system does not only react to germs. Sometimes it reacts to things that are not harmful at all. This overreaction is what we call an allergy.

Imagine the immune system as a security guard. When a real thief enters, the guard raises an alarm and protects the house. But sometimes the guard raises an alarm even when a harmless guest arrives. The guest is not a thief, but the guard thinks it is. In the same way, during an allergy, the immune system treats harmless substances such as dust, pollen, or certain foods as if they were dangerous germs. The "false alarm" releases chemicals, especially histamine, which cause symptoms like sneezing, itching, runny nose, watering eyes, or skin rash. So the first idea to master is the definition: an allergy is an overreaction of the body's immune system to normally harmless substances.

Now let us think about the substances that cause this overreaction. These are called allergens. An allergen is the trigger, the thing that starts the allergic reaction. You should be able to list common allergens from your daily life. Dust is everywhere -- on shelves, in old books, on curtains, and on floors. Pollen grains are tiny, light, powdery particles produced by flowers and grasses; they float in the air, especially during spring and early summer, and can be seen floating in sunlight near a window. Dust mites are microscopic creatures that live in house dust, mattresses, pillows, carpets, and upholstery. Strong sunlight, especially the ultraviolet part, can trigger a skin reaction in some sensitive people. Particular food items can also act as allergens; shellfish such as prawns, crabs, and lobsters, and nuts such as peanuts and cashew nuts, are common examples. Notice that these foods are nutritious for most people, but in some individuals they cause an allergic response.

A good answer for an allergen is "pollen grains from flowering plants, which are inhaled through the nose." A weak answer would simply say "pollen" without explaining what it is or how it enters the body. Another weak answer would confuse an allergen with a pathogen and say "bacteria cause allergy," which is not correct because bacteria cause communicable diseases, not allergies. When you describe an allergen, always name the substance and, where possible, explain that it is harmless to most people but causes an overreaction in sensitive individuals.

Next, let us look at how allergens enter the body. The three main entry routes are through the mouth, the nose, and the skin. When someone eats a food allergen such as shellfish or nuts, the allergen enters through the mouth. When a person breathes in dust, pollen, or tiny particles from dust mites, the allergen enters through the nose. This is why a dusty room or a field full of flowering grasses can make a person sneeze. When the skin touches an irritant, such as certain plants, strong sunlight, or chemicals in soaps, cosmetics, or fabrics, the allergen enters through the skin and may cause a red, itchy rash. In India, children in cities like Delhi may notice more dust allergies in the dry winter, while those in coastal regions like Kochi or Chennai may encounter shellfish more often, which can trigger food allergies in sensitive children. Children in open, grassy areas or near mustard and neem fields may experience pollen-related sneezing.

It is very important not to mix up the allergen and the allergy. The allergen is the trigger or cause. The allergy is the reaction or effect. For example, dust is an allergen; the sneezing and coughing that follow are the allergy. Pollen is an allergen; the watering eyes and runny nose are the allergy. Shellfish is an allergen; the skin rash or stomach upset is the allergy. A strong answer in the exam will clearly say: "An allergen is the substance that causes an allergic reaction, while an allergy is the body's response to that substance." A weak answer will use the two words as if they mean the same thing, which will cost marks.

Let us also understand the role of histamine. When the immune system detects an allergen, the body releases a chemical called histamine. Histamine is not harmful in itself, but it causes blood vessels to widen and fluids to leak into nearby tissues. This produces swelling, redness, itching, and mucus. That is why an antihistamine medicine is sometimes given to reduce allergy symptoms; it blocks the effect of histamine. However, you do not need to memorise medicines for this topic; you only need to know that histamine is the chemical released during an allergic reaction.

In the ICSE Class 7 board examination, you can expect direct, simple questions from this node because it is at the "Remember" cognitive level and the difficulty is easy. The examiner may ask you to define allergy, to list common allergens, or to identify the three entry routes. The examiner will also check whether you can distinguish between an allergen and an allergy. From the board exam analysis, examiners have noticed that students sometimes confuse similar terms, such as food adulterants and food additives, or GDP and GNP, because the names look alike. In the same way, "allergen" and "allergy" are similar words, and you must be careful not to mix them. A neat answer with a clear example will earn full marks. Always write in complete sentences and label the allergen and the allergy separately when asked for definitions.

The thing that sets off the alarm is called an allergen. Allergens can come into your body through your mouth, nose, or skin.

Correction: an allergen is the trigger substance; an allergy is the body's reaction to that substance. Dust is the allergen, but sneezing is the allergy.

Misconception 2: Some students think all allergies are caused by germs, because they remember from Class 6 that diseases are caused by pathogens. This is not true for allergies. Correction: an allergy is an overreaction of the immune system to harmless substances such as pollen, dust, or food. It is not an infection, and it is not spread from person to person.

Smoke may irritate the nose, but it is not the same as an allergen. Correction: common allergens for this syllabus are dust, pollen grains, dust mites, strong sunlight, and particular food items such as shellfish and nuts.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Define allergy and give any four common examples of allergens.
Answer: Allergy is an overreaction of the body's immune system to substances that are normally harmless. In other words, the immune system mistakes a harmless substance for a dangerous enemy and releases chemicals such as histamine, which cause symptoms like sneezing, runny nose, watering eyes, itching, or skin rash. An allergen is the substance that triggers this reaction. Four common examples of allergens are dust, pollen grains, dust mites, and particular food items such as shellfish and nuts. Dust is present in homes, schools, and libraries, especially on old books and curtains. Pollen grains are tiny particles released by flowers and grasses; they float in the air and can be inhaled through the nose. Dust mites are microscopic organisms that live in dust, mattresses, carpets, and upholstery. Shellfish and nuts such as peanuts and cashew nuts can cause allergic reactions when eaten by sensitive people. Other examples include strong sunlight, which can affect the skin, and animal dander. To score well, the definition should clearly say that the body's immune system is reacting to a harmless substance, and the examples should be drawn from the syllabus list.

Q2 (reasoning): Explain the difference between an allergen and an allergy, using one example from each of the three entry routes: mouth, nose, and skin.
Answer: An allergen is the substance that causes an allergic reaction, while an allergy is the body's response to that substance. The allergen is the cause or trigger; the allergy is the effect or set of symptoms. For the mouth, the allergen is a particular food item such as a peanut or shellfish, and the allergy is the stomach discomfort or skin rash that appears after eating it. For the nose, the allergen is dust or pollen grains floating in the air, and the allergy is sneezing, a runny nose, and watering eyes. For the skin, the allergen may be strong sunlight, a chemical in soap, or contact with a plant, and the allergy is a red, itchy rash or irritation on the skin. It is important not to mix the two terms in the examination. If the question asks for an allergen, the correct answer should name the trigger, such as "dust" or "pollen." If the question asks for an allergy, the correct answer should describe the reaction, such as "sneezing" or "skin rash." Using the terms correctly shows that the student has understood the distinction between the cause and the effect.

Q3 (evaluate): "Pollen is a harmful substance because it causes allergies in many people." Do you agree with this statement? Give reasons for your answer.
Answer: This statement is partly true but not completely correct, so it should be evaluated carefully. It is true that pollen can cause allergic reactions in some people. When a sensitive person inhales pollen grains through the nose, the immune system may overreact and release histamine, leading to sneezing, runny nose, and watering eyes. In this sense, pollen is an allergen for those people. However, pollen is not a harmful or dangerous substance in itself. It is a natural, harmless, and even useful part of the environment. Pollen is produced by flowers and is essential for plant reproduction because it helps in the process of pollination. Without pollen, many plants would not be able to produce seeds and fruits. For most people, pollen does not cause any problem at all. Only individuals who have a sensitivity or an overactive immune response to pollen experience allergies. Therefore, it would be wrong to say that pollen is harmful in general. It is more accurate to say that pollen is a harmless substance that triggers an allergic reaction in certain sensitive individuals. This is the key idea of the chapter: the immune system can overreact to normally harmless substances, and the substance itself is not the enemy. A balanced answer should accept the link between pollen and allergy, but also explain that pollen is not harmful by nature and plays a useful role in the life of plants.

Q4 (apply): Rina starts sneezing and her eyes begin to water whenever she sits near the open window during the spring mornings. She also gets a red rash on her skin when she eats prawns. Identify the likely allergens and the entry routes in each case. Suggest simple precautions she could take.
Answer: In the first situation, when Rina sits near the open window during spring mornings and starts sneezing with watering eyes, the likely allergen is pollen. In spring, many flowers and grasses release pollen grains into the air. The pollen enters Rina's body through the nose, which is the inhalation or nasal route. In the second situation, the red rash on her skin after eating prawns is caused by shellfish, which is a food allergen. The prawn allergen enters through the mouth, which is the ingestion or oral route, and the reaction appears on the skin as a rash. To reduce the pollen allergy, Rina could keep the windows closed during early morning hours, use a clean handkerchief, avoid going to grassy or flowering areas during high pollen times, and wash her face and hands after being outdoors. For the food allergy, she should avoid eating prawns and other shellfish, read food labels when eating outside, and inform her family and school about her sensitivity so that she is not served shellfish accidentally. These precautions target the entry routes: avoiding inhalation of pollen and avoiding ingestion of shellfish.

Q5 (create): Design a small poster or chart for your school health club titled "Know Your Allergens." What information and pictures would you include, and how would you explain the three entry routes clearly to younger students?
Answer: The poster "Know Your Allergens" should have a bold title at the top and a friendly, colourful layout. In the first section, I would define allergy in simple terms: "An allergy is a false alarm in the body. The immune system thinks a harmless thing is dangerous and makes us sneeze, cough, or get a rash." The second section would show common allergens with pictures: a cloud of dust near old books, tiny pollen grains floating in the air, dust mites under a magnifying glass, a sun symbol for strong sunlight, and pictures of shellfish and nuts such as peanuts. The third section would clearly explain the three entry routes using labelled diagrams. For the mouth, I would draw a child eating a peanut with a cross over it and the words: "Food allergens enter through the mouth." For the nose, I would draw a child breathing in pollen or dust with the words: "Dust and pollen enter through the nose." For the skin, I would draw a hand touching sunlight and a plant with the words: "Sunlight and touch allergens enter through the skin." I would also include a "Good vs Bad" example box showing: "Good: Shellfish is the allergen, and the skin rash is the allergy." and "Bad: Allergy and allergen mean the same thing." At the bottom, I would add a safety tip: "If you often sneeze, cough, or get a rash, tell a parent, teacher, or doctor." This poster would help younger students remember the definition, the examples, and the three entry routes visually and clearly.

title: Communicable diseases (detailed)
definition: A communicable disease is an illness caused by a pathogen that can pass from one infected person, animal, or object to another. In this node you study six important examples in detail: influenza, measles, malaria, dengue, chikungunya, and HIV. For each disease you must know its causative agent, its mode of transmission, its key symptoms, and its prevention methods. You also need the special idea of a vector: a living organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without itself falling ill. The female Anopheles mosquito is the vector for malaria, because it carries the protozoan parasite Plasmodium from the blood of one human to another. The Aedes aegypti mosquito is the vector for both dengue and chikungunya, which are viral diseases. Influenza and measles are contagious diseases that spread through direct contact or through tiny droplets released when an infected person coughs or sneezes; they do not need a vector. HIV is caused by a retrovirus and is spread mainly through infected blood, unprotected sexual contact, from an infected mother to her baby, and by the sharing of contaminated needles or syringes. Symptoms vary: influenza brings sudden fever, cough, sore throat and body ache; measles brings fever, cough, runny nose, tiny white spots inside the mouth called Koplik spots and a red rash; malaria shows fever with chills and sweating that often follows a cycle; dengue causes high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, and sometimes skin rash; chikungunya causes fever with severe joint pain; HIV infection may first look like flu, then remain silent for years before weakening the immune system and leading to AIDS. Prevention includes keeping hands, food and water clean, covering the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing, avoiding close contact with sick people, using mosquito nets and repellents, removing stagnant water around homes, and avoiding shared needles, unscreened blood products, and unsafe sexual contact. Sanitation and vector control are therefore central to protecting communities in India, where monsoon rains often create breeding places for mosquitoes.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin with what you already know. In the earlier node c6_bio_021 you learned that diseases can travel from person to person through air, water, food, and insects. That was like learning the different roads a disease can take. Now, in Class 8, we are going to drive along each road and meet the exact traveller: the pathogen and, where it applies, the vector that carries it. Think of a pathogen as the actual criminal and a vector as the unwitting getaway vehicle.

First, consider the two contagious diseases. Influenza is caused by the influenza virus and moves through droplets and direct contact. When someone with influenza coughs, thousands of tiny droplets spread into the air and can be breathed in by others or land on surfaces and then on hands. Measles, also a viral disease, is one of the most contagious illnesses known; a single child with measles can infect many classmates through coughs and sneezes. The virus first causes fever, cough and cold-like symptoms, then a rash that spreads over the body. These are not vector-borne; they pass directly from one human to another.

Now look at the vector-borne trio. Malaria is caused by a protozoan, Plasmodium, not by a virus or bacteria. The female Anopheles mosquito bites an infected person, takes up the parasite, and later bites a healthy person to pass it on. Dengue and chikungunya are both caused by viruses, and both are spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which breeds in clean, stagnant water such as water in flowerpots, old tyres, and uncovered tanks. In cities like Delhi, Ahmedabad and Kolkata, outbreaks often rise soon after the monsoon because such breeding spots multiply rapidly.

HIV stands apart. It is caused by a retrovirus, Human Immunodeficiency Virus, and it attacks the immune system. It does not spread through air, water, food, mosquitoes, hugging, or sharing a classroom. It spreads through infected blood, semen, vaginal fluids, and breast milk. In India, the National AIDS Control Organisation works to prevent HIV by promoting safe blood transfusion, safe practices, and awareness.

Here is a good and bad answer comparison. A good answer to "How does malaria spread?" says: "Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and is transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito." A weak answer says: "Malaria is caused by a mosquito." The first is correct because it names both the pathogen and the vector. Another good answer: "Dengue and chikungunya are spread by the Aedes aegypti mosquito." A bad answer: "All mosquitoes cause all fevers." Diseases are specific; each has its own causative agent and vector.

In the ICSE board exam, expect short questions that ask you to name the causative agent and mode of transmission for each disease, or to draw a clear distinction between contagious and vector-borne diseases. Examiners want exact names: "Plasmodium" not "germ," "Aedes aegypti" not just "mosquito." They also want accurate, well-spelled terminology and correct associations, such as malaria with Anopheles and dengue with Aedes.
eli5: Communicable diseases are sicknesses that jump from one person to another. Some hop through cough drops and sneezes, like influenza and measles. Some need a mosquito as a delivery truck, like malaria, dengue and chikungunya. HIV moves through infected blood or close body contact. We can stop them by washing hands, blocking mosquitoes, and never sharing needles.
misconceptionText:
Misconception 1: Writing only "virus" or "bacteria" as the causative agent. The board examiner observations for 2024 note that many candidates used general terms like "bacteria" and "virus" and did not give the specific causative agent. The correction is to learn the exact pathogen for each disease: influenza virus for influenza, measles virus for measles, Plasmodium for malaria, dengue virus for dengue, chikungunya virus for chikungunya, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus for HIV.

Misconception 2: Confusing the vector with the disease itself, or using the word "mosquito" without naming the correct species. Several candidates wrote "Anopheles/Aedes mosquito" or simply "mosquito" when a more specific vector was expected. The correction is to remember that the female Anopheles mosquito carries malaria, while the Aedes aegypti mosquito carries dengue and chikungunya. Calling every fever "dengue" or "chikungunya" is also a common mistake; each disease has a specific pattern of fever, rash, and joint pain.

Misconception 3: Mixing up HIV and AIDS with other diseases. The board exam guidances note that some candidates mentioned dengue, chikungunya, or common cough and cold when asked about AIDS, and some confused the symptoms of sexually transmitted diseases with those of AIDS. The correction is to keep the distinction clear: HIV is the virus that causes the infection; AIDS is the advanced stage in which the immune system becomes very weak. HIV is not spread by mosquitoes, sharing food, or casual contact.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): For each of the six diseases listed in the syllabus, name the causative agent, the mode of transmission, and the vector if one is involved.
Answer: Influenza is caused by the influenza virus and spreads through droplet infection and direct contact when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or touches surfaces. Measles is caused by the measles virus and also spreads through droplets and close contact, making it highly contagious. Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium and is transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. Dengue is caused by the dengue virus and is transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito. Chikungunya is caused by the chikungunya virus and is transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, and sometimes by Aedes albopictus. HIV is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus, a retrovirus, and is transmitted through infected blood, unprotected sexual contact, from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding, and by sharing contaminated needles or syringes. None of these last three diseases use a human sneeze as their main route; only influenza and measles do.

Q2 (reasoning): A vector is often compared to an unwitting delivery person. Using malaria, dengue, or chikungunya as an example, explain why the mosquito is called a vector and not the causative agent.
Answer: A vector is an organism that carries the pathogen from one host to another without itself suffering from the disease. The mosquito is not the disease-causing organism; it is the carrier. In malaria, the real causative agent is the protozoan Plasmodium. When a female Anopheles mosquito bites an infected person, the parasite enters the mosquito and develops inside it. The mosquito does not fall ill with malaria; it simply carries the parasite in its salivary glands. When the same mosquito bites a healthy person, it injects saliva containing the parasite, and the new person becomes infected. Similarly, the Aedes aegypti mosquito carries the viruses that cause dengue and chikungunya but the mosquito itself does not show the symptoms of these diseases. This is why we say the mosquito is a vector, not the causative agent. The causative agent is the pathogen that actually produces the disease, while the vector is the transport system.

Q3 (evaluate): "All communicable diseases are spread by mosquitoes, so mosquito control alone can prevent every communicable disease." Evaluate this statement.
Answer: This statement is not correct, although it does contain a small amount of truth. It is true that some serious communicable diseases, such as malaria, dengue and chikungunya, are spread by mosquitoes, and that controlling these insects is very important for preventing those diseases. However, the statement is false for several reasons. First, many communicable diseases are not vector-borne at all. Influenza and measles spread through droplets and direct contact, so they can pass from one child to another in a classroom without any mosquito. HIV spreads through infected blood, sexual contact, and from mother to child, not through insect bites. Second, even if we remove every mosquito, diseases such as influenza could still spread through coughs and sneezes, and HIV could still spread through unsafe practices. Third, effective prevention needs different strategies for different diseases: handwashing and covering the mouth for influenza and measles, safe blood and needle practices for HIV, and sanitation and mosquito control for vector-borne diseases. Therefore, mosquito control is essential but not sufficient for all communicable diseases.

Q4 (apply): You live in a village in a malaria-endemic region of India. List five practical steps you and your family can take to reduce the risk of malaria and dengue, and explain why each step works.
Answer: The first step is to sleep under insecticide-treated mosquito nets, because the female Anopheles mosquito that carries malaria bites mostly at night, and the net forms a physical barrier. The second step is to remove or cover all stagnant water around the house, such as water in discarded tyres, flowerpots, broken bottles, and uncovered tanks, because the Aedes aegypti mosquito that spreads dengue and chikungunya breeds in clean, still water. The third step is to wear long-sleeved clothes and apply mosquito repellent in the evening, especially during the monsoon, to reduce the chance of being bitten. The fourth step is to keep doors and windows screened or closed at dusk and dawn to stop mosquitoes from entering. The fifth step is to seek early diagnosis and complete the full course of anti-malarial medicine if fever occurs, because prompt treatment prevents the disease from becoming severe and stops the infected person from becoming a source of parasites for mosquitoes.

Q5 (create): Design a school awareness poster on communicable diseases that clearly separates contagious diseases, vector-borne diseases, and blood-borne diseases. What headings, pictures, and prevention messages would you include, and why?
Answer: The poster would be divided into three colour-coded sections. The first section, in yellow, would be labelled "Spread through the air and close contact" and would show a child covering a sneeze with a handkerchief, representing influenza and measles. The prevention message would read "Cover your mouth and nose, wash your hands, and stay away from school if you have fever." The second section, in red, would be labelled "Spread by mosquitoes" and would show a mosquito, a water pot with a lid, and a bed net, representing malaria, dengue and chikungunya. The message would read "Remove stagnant water, use nets and repellents, and wear full sleeves." The third section, in blue, would be labelled "Spread through blood and body fluids" and would show a red cross over a shared syringe and a blood donation bag, representing HIV. The message would read "Use safe blood, do not share needles, and follow safe practices." This design helps students see that not every communicable disease spreads the same way, and that prevention must match the route of transmission.
masteryCriteria: Can name three communicable diseases (malaria, tuberculosis, cholera) and their causative agents (mosquito, bacteria, bacteria); can state the mode of transmission for each; can describe two ways to prevent communicable diseases (vaccination, hygiene).
